before.quote: Fix $n\ge1$, an objective oracle $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{\text{nonfinite}\}$, a finite integer call budget $B\ge0$, positive tolerances $\varepsilon_x,\varepsilon_f$, and an ordered initial simplex $(v_0,\ldots,v_n)$. Call the ordered tuple nondegenerate when, for real coefficients $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$, $\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i(v_i-v_0)=0$ implies every $\lambda_i=0$. Use reflection $\alpha=1$, expansion $\gamma=2$, contraction $\rho=1/2$, and shrink $\sigma=1/2$. Ties in sorting objective values are broken by current vertex slot, lower slot first. When recording the best point seen, replace it only on a strict objective improvement, so ties retain the earliest evaluation; initial vertices are evaluated in slot order.

If the initial simplex is degenerate, return **degenerate-simplex**. If $B<n+1$, return **budget-exhausted** with zero calls and no best point. Otherwise evaluate initial vertices in slot order, counting every call. A nonfinite result returns **nonfinite-objective** and the best finite point seen, if any. For each committed simplex, let $x_b$ be its sorted best vertex, $x_w$ its worst, let $x_2$ denote the second-worst (the best when $n=1$), and set $c:=n^{-1}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}x_i$ using the sorted vertices $x_0,\ldots,x_n$. Define the diameter $D=\max_{0\le i,j\le n}\|x_i-x_j\|_2$, and spread $S=f(x_w)-f(x_b)$. Stop with **tolerance-met** exactly when both $D\le\varepsilon_x$ and $S\le\varepsilon_f$.

before.quote: Let $n\ge1$ and let $D=(d_1,\ldots,d_m)$ be a nonempty finite ordered list in $\mathbb R^n$. It is **positive spanning** if every $w\in\mathbb R^n$ has a representation $w=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i d_i$ with $\lambda_i\ge0$. Keep the order to make a deterministic poll. Define the directional score $\psi_D(v)=\max_{1\le i\le m}(-\langle v,d_i\rangle)$ for unit $v$, and the largest poll norm $D_{\max}=\max_{1\le i\le m}\|d_i\|_2$. A positive uniform lower bound for $\psi_D$ is a separate theorem, not part of this definition.

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.

   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

## Definition
Finite sums of vectors in $\mathbb R^n$ use the additive finite-list sum of [[def-linear-combination-and-span]]; sums of real coefficients use [[def-finite-sum]].

Fix $n\ge1$, an objective oracle $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{\text{nonfinite}\}$, a finite integer call budget $B\ge0$, positive tolerances $\varepsilon_x,\varepsilon_f$, and an ordered initial simplex $(v_0,\ldots,v_n)$. Call the ordered tuple nondegenerate when, for real coefficients $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$, $\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i(v_i-v_0)=0$ implies every $\lambda_i=0$. Use reflection $\alpha=1$, expansion $\gamma=2$, contraction $\rho=1/2$, and shrink $\sigma=1/2$. Ties in sorting objective values are broken by current vertex slot, lower slot first. When recording the best point seen, replace it only on a strict objective improvement, so ties retain the earliest evaluation; initial vertices are evaluated in slot order.

If the initial simplex is degenerate, return **degenerate-simplex**. If $B<n+1$, return **budget-exhausted** with zero calls and no best point. Otherwise evaluate initial vertices in slot order, counting every call. A nonfinite result returns **nonfinite-objective** and the best finite point seen, if any. For each committed simplex, let $x_b$ be its sorted best vertex, $x_w$ its worst, let $x_2$ denote the second-worst (the best when $n=1$), and set $c:=n^{-1}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}x_i$ using the sorted vertices $x_0,\ldots,x_n$. Define the diameter $D=\max_{0\le i,j\le n}\|x_i-x_j\|_2$, and spread $S=f(x_w)-f(x_b)$. Stop with **tolerance-met** exactly when both $D\le\varepsilon_x$ and $S\le\varepsilon_f$.

Otherwise evaluate reflection $x_r=c+(c-x_w)$. If $f(x_r)<f(x_b)$, evaluate expansion $x_e=c+2(x_r-c)$ and replace $x_w$ by $x_e$ iff $f(x_e)<f(x_r)$; a tie keeps reflection. If $f(x_b)\le f(x_r)<f(x_2)$, where $x_2$ is the second-worst vertex, replace $x_w$ by reflection. If $f(x_2)\le f(x_r)<f(x_w)$, evaluate outside contraction $x_{oc}=c+(x_r-c)/2$ and accept iff $f(x_{oc})\le f(x_r)$; equality accepts. If $f(x_r)\ge f(x_w)$, evaluate inside contraction $x_{ic}=c+(x_w-c)/2$ and accept iff $f(x_{ic})<f(x_w)$; equality fails. A failed contraction shrinks each nonbest vertex to $x_b+(v_i-x_b)/2$.

Count every objective call, including rejected trials. Before a needed call, if the budget is exhausted, return **budget-exhausted** with the last committed simplex and best finite point seen; do not partially commit an update. A nonfinite trial returns **nonfinite-objective** with the same committed simplex. If a proposed complete update is degenerate, return **degenerate-simplex** without committing it. After a valid update, recheck both tolerances. No general convergence guarantee is asserted.

Let $n\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex. The finite-budget projected subgradient procedure takes $x_0\in C$, an integer budget $N\ge1$, and positive stepsizes $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{N-1}$. At iteration $k$, an oracle returns either failure or a pair $(f(x_k),g_k)$ with $g_k\in\partial f(x_k)$, where subgradient has the meaning in [[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]]. On a valid response set
$$x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k g_k),$$
where $P_C(u)$ is the unique nearest point in $C$ to $u$. On an oracle failure at iteration $k$, return status **oracle-failure**, the feasible current iterate, the completed update count, and the least-index best among values observed so far if any (otherwise report none); a full-horizon average is not returned. If all $N$ calls succeed, return status **budget-exhausted**, the final iterate, the weighted average $\bar x_N=(\sum_{k<N}\alpha_kx_k)/(\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k)$, and a least-index minimizer of observed values among $x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1}$. ## Statement

For every finite positive-spanning list $D=(d_1,\ldots,d_m)$ in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$, the score $\psi_D(v)=\max_i(-\langle v,d_i\rangle)$ on the unit sphere attains a strictly positive minimum. Write this minimum as $\kappa_D>0$. Thus for every $v\in\mathbb R^n$ there is $d_i\in D$ with $-\langle v,d_i\rangle\ge\kappa_D\|v\|_2$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Positive spanning and directional score [[def-positive-spanning-poll-set-and-angle]], Euclidean geometry [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], compactness and extrema ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

[F1] For every unit vector $u$, positive spanning writes $-u=\sum_i\lambda_i d_i$ with $\lambda_i\ge0$ ([[def-positive-spanning-poll-set-and-angle]]).

[F2] Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\langle u,d_i\rangle|\le\|u\|_2\|d_i\|_2$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]).

[F3] By the coordinatewise vector-sum convention, $\langle u,\sum_i\lambda_i d_i\rangle=\sum_{k<n}u_k\sum_{j<m}\lambda_{j+1}(d_{j+1})_k$. Finite distributivity and reordering the two finite sums, using finite-sum additivity/scaling and induction on their lengths, gives $\sum_i\lambda_i\langle u,d_i\rangle$. A finite sum of nonnegative real terms is nonnegative ([[def-positive-spanning-poll-set-and-angle]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

[F4] If $M=\max_i|a_i-b_i|$ for two nonempty finite lists, then $a_i\le b_i+M\le\max_jb_j+M$ for each $i$; taking maxima and reversing the lists gives $|\max_i a_i-\max_i b_i|\le M$ ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

[F5] The unit sphere is nonempty, closed, and bounded. For $n\ge1$, the standard vector $e_0$ has Euclidean norm $1$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). If $\|x\|_2\ne1$, choose $\varepsilon=|\|x\|_2-1|/2$; the reverse triangle inequality shows every $y$ with $d_2(x,y)<\varepsilon$ also has $\|y\|_2\ne1$, so the complement is open. Every unit vector lies in $B_2(0,2)$, so the sphere is bounded. Hence it is compact by Heine–Borel ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], [[def-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]], [[def-metric-ball]], [[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

[F6] [[thm-reals-ordered-field]] makes $\mathbb R$ a totally ordered field, in particular the product of two strictly positive reals is positive; [[lem-of-zero-mult]] gives multiplication by zero. Hence if $a,b\ge0$, either one is zero and $ab=0$ (using field commutativity if needed), or both are strictly positive and $ab>0$. Thus $ab\ge0$.

## Proof

1.1 Taking inner products of [F1] with $u$ and using [F3] gives $-1=\sum_i\lambda_i\langle u,d_i\rangle$. Since all $\lambda_i\ge0$, at least one index with positive coefficient has $\langle u,d_i\rangle<0$; otherwise every summand is nonnegative by [F6] and [F3] makes the sum nonnegative, a contradiction. Hence $\psi_D(u)>0$ for every unit $u$. [F1, F3, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F4], $|\psi_D(u)-\psi_D(w)|\le\max_i|\langle u-w,d_i\rangle|$, and [F2] bounds the right side by $D_{\max}\|u-w\|_2$, so the score is continuous. ## Statement

The relation of [[def-real-order]] is well defined and makes $\mathbb{R}$
([[thm-reals-field]]) a totally ordered field.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Reals $x, y$ with representatives $(a_n), (b_n)$.

[L1] A sequence $(u_n)_{n \ge 1}$ of rational numbers is null if, for every rational $\varepsilon > 0$, there is $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $|u_n| < \varepsilon$ for every $n \ge N$ ([[def-null-sequence]]).

[L2] Ordered-field arithmetic in $\mathbb{Q}$: $\delta/2 > 0$; sums and products of eventual lower bounds ([[thm-rat-ordered-field]]).

[L3] Dichotomy for non-null Cauchy sequences: eventually $> \delta$ or eventually $< -\delta$ ([[lem-cauchy-away-from-zero]]).

[L4] $\mathbb{R}$ is a field ([[thm-reals-field]]).

[L5] In $\mathbb{R} = \mathcal{C}/\mathcal{N}$, $x = 0$ iff a representative is null; so $x \ne 0$ iff every representative is non-null ([[def-real-numbers]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Positivity is independent of the representative: if $a_n > \delta$ for $n \ge N$ and $(a'_n - a_n)$ is null, then beyond some $N' \ge N$ also $|a'_n - a_n| < \delta/2$, so $a'_n > \delta/2$: the defining property holds for $(a'_n)$ with $\delta/2$. [L1, L2]

1.2 Trichotomy: if $x \ne 0$, any representative is non-null, so by the dichotomy either $a_n > \delta$ eventually ($x$ positive) or $a_n < -\delta$ eventually ($-x$ positive); the two exclude each other, and exactly one of $x$ positive, $x = 0$, $-x$ positive holds. [L1, L3, L5]

1.3 Positives are closed under $+$ and $\cdot$: from $a_n > \delta$ and $b_n > \delta'$ eventually, $a_n + b_n > \delta + \delta'$ and $a_n b_n > \delta\delta'$ eventually, with $\delta + \delta', \delta\delta' > 0$. [L2]

2.1 Consequently $\le$ is a total order (trichotomy plus transitivity from closure under sums), compatible with addition (translation preserves the difference) and with multiplication by positives: $\mathbb{R}$ is a totally ordered field. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, L4] ∎

## Statement

In any field $F$ ([[def-field]]), for every $a \in F$ we have $0 \cdot a = 0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$ and an element $a \in F$.

[L1] Field axioms ([[def-field]]): $0$ is the additive identity, so $0 + 0 = 0$ and $x + 0 = x$ for all $x$; multiplication distributes over addition, $(y + z) \cdot x = y \cdot x + z \cdot x$.

[L2] Field axioms ([[def-field]]): every element has an additive inverse, so addition admits cancellation: if $x + z = y + z$ then $x = y$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Since $0 + 0 = 0$, we have $0 \cdot a = (0 + 0) \cdot a$. [L1]

1.2 By distributivity, $(0 + 0) \cdot a = 0 \cdot a + 0 \cdot a$. [L1]

1.3 Since $0$ is the additive identity, $0 \cdot a = 0 \cdot a + 0$. [L1]

2.1 Combining the two expressions for $(0 + 0) \cdot a$ gives $0 \cdot a = 0 \cdot a + 0 \cdot a$. [step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 From steps 1.3 and 2.1, $0 \cdot a + 0 = 0 \cdot a + 0 \cdot a$. [step 1.3, step 2.1]

4.1 Cancelling $0 \cdot a$ from both sides yields $0 = 0 \cdot a$, that is $0 \cdot a = 0$. [step 3.1, L2] ∎

## Statement

Let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex. For a positive finite family of points in $C$ and nonnegative weights summing to one, $f$ of their weighted Euclidean sum is at most the weighted sum of their $f$-values. Explicitly, if $N\ge1$, $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in C$, $\lambda_j\ge0$, and $\sum_{j=1}^N\lambda_j=1$, then

$$f\left(\sum_{j=1}^N\lambda_jx_j\right)\le\sum_{j=1}^N\lambda_jf(x_j).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The data in the Statement, the finite-sum convention [[def-finite-sum]], its algebraic laws [[lem-finite-sum-laws]], and induction on the positive integer $N$ [[thm-induction-principle]].

[F1] The function $f:C\to\mathbb R$ is convex when $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)$ for all $x,y\in C$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]).

[F2] Finite vector sums and linear combinations in $\mathbb R^n$ use [[def-linear-combination-and-span]], with its zero-based finite-list convention reindexed here as $1,\ldots,N$. The domain $C$ of the convex function is convex by [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]: it contains $(1-t)x+ty$ for $x,y\in C$ and $0\le t\le1$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** induction.

1.1 We prove simultaneously that each such weighted sum belongs to $C$ and satisfies the stated inequality. For $N=1$, $\lambda_1=1$, so the vector sum is $x_1\in C$ and both sides equal $f(x_1)$. [F1, F2, algebra, base]

1.2 Fix $N\ge1$ and assume both membership in $C$ and the inequality for every weighted family of $N$ points. [ih]

2.1 For $N+1$ points, if $\lambda_{N+1}=1$, then all earlier nonnegative weights vanish, the vector sum is $x_{N+1}\in C$, and the inequality is equality. Otherwise $s=1-\lambda_{N+1}>0$, and the normalized weights $\mu_j=\lambda_j/s$ for $j\le N$ are nonnegative and sum to one. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 By the simultaneous induction hypothesis, $z=\sum_{j=1}^N\mu_jx_j$ belongs to $C$ and $f(z)\le\sum_{j=1}^N\mu_jf(x_j)$. Since $s=1-\lambda_{N+1}$, $0\le\lambda_{N+1}<1$, and $z,x_{N+1}\in C$, convexity of $C$ in [F2] puts $w=sz+\lambda_{N+1}x_{N+1}$ in $C$. The finite-vector-sum recursion and distributivity identify $w=\sum_{j=1}^{N+1}\lambda_jx_j$. Applying [F1] gives $f(w)\le s f(z)+\lambda_{N+1}f(x_{N+1})\le\sum_{j=1}^{N+1}\lambda_jf(x_j)$. Thus both membership and the inequality hold at $N+1$, completing the induction. [step 1.2, step 2.1, F1, F2, algebra, discharge-induction] ∎

## Statement

Let $K$ be compact in Euclidean $\mathbb R^n$ and let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $K\subseteq V$. There is $\delta>0$ such that for every $x\in K$, if $\|y-x\|_2<\delta$, then $y\in V$. If $K=\emptyset$, any positive $\delta$ works.

[F2] Every open cover of compact $K$ has a finite subcover ([[def-metric-compactness]], [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]]).

[F3] A nonempty finite set of real numbers has a minimum that belongs to the set ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

## Statement

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be totally differentiable at every point, and suppose its gradient is $L$-Lipschitz on $U$ for some $L\ge0$. If $x,y\in U$ and the whole segment $[x,y]$ lies in $U$, then
$$f(y)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\|y-x\|_2^2.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Total derivatives and gradients [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]], the Lipschitz definition and Euclidean metric [[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], local continuity of totally differentiable maps [[thm-total-differentiability-gives-a-local-linear-bound-and-continuity]], Cauchy–Schwarz [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], derivative rules [[def-derivative]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], and the mean-value theorem [[cor-mean-value-theorem]].

[F1] The Lipschitz condition is $d_2(\nabla f(u),\nabla f(v))\le Ld_2(u,v)$; for $n\ge1$, $d_2(a,b)=\|a-b\|_2$ ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

[F2] A real function continuous on a closed interval and differentiable in its interior has a point where its derivative equals its secant slope ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).

[F3] Total differentiability implies continuity, and the directional derivative along $d$ is $D_df(a)=\langle\nabla f(a),d\rangle$ ([[thm-total-differentiability-gives-a-local-linear-bound-and-continuity]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]).

[F4] The identity function has derivative $1$ by its difference quotient; the sum, scalar-multiple, and product rules follow from [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], and restricting a differentiable function to an interval preserves its interior derivatives ([[def-derivative]]).

[F5] Cauchy–Schwarz and norm homogeneity give $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$ and $\|sv\|_2=|s|\|v\|_2$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]).

[F6] Sums, scalar multiples, products, and polynomials of continuous real functions are continuous ([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]).

## Proof

1.1 Put $d=y-x$. If $d=0$, both sides are equal. For $d\ne0$, necessarily $n\ge1$. Define $\gamma(s)=x+sd$ and $I=\{s\in\mathbb R:\gamma(s)\in U\}$. Since $\|\gamma(s+h)-\gamma(s)\|_2=|h|\|d\|_2$, the affine path is continuous; openness of $U$ then makes $I$ open, and the segment assumption gives $[0,1]\subseteq I$. Put $\phi=f\circ\gamma$ on $I$. Total differentiability makes $f$ continuous at every point of $\gamma([0,1])$, so $\phi$ is continuous on $[0,1]$. For each $s\in(0,1)$, its difference quotient is the directional difference quotient of $f$ at $x+sd$ in direction $d$, so $\phi'(s)=\langle\nabla f(x+sd),d\rangle$. [given, F3, F5, construct]

2.1 Put $a=\langle\nabla f(x),d\rangle$, $g(s)=\phi(s)-\phi(0)-sa$, and $q(s)=g(s)-\frac{L}{2}s^2\|d\|_2^2$. By [F3] and [F6], $q$ is continuous on $[0,1]$; by [F4], it is differentiable on $(0,1)$ and
$$q'(s)=\langle\nabla f(x+sd)-\nabla f(x),d\rangle-Ls\|d\|_2^2.$$
By [F1] and [F5], the inner-product term is at most $L\|sd\|_2\|d\|_2=Ls\|d\|_2^2$ for $s\in(0,1)$. Hence $q'(s)\le0$. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F2] to $q$ on $[0,1]$: for some $s\in(0,1)$, $q(1)-q(0)=q'(s)\le0$. Since $q(0)=0$, this says $f(y)-f(x)-\langle\nabla f(x),d\rangle\le\frac{L}{2}\|d\|_2^2$, as required. [F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Every invocation of [[alg-nelder-mead-finite-budget]] with finite call budget $B$ returns a status after at most $B$ objective calls. ## Statement

Let $N\ge1$ be an integer and run [[alg-projected-subgradient-method]] with all stated inputs. Every execution returns after at most $N$ oracle calls. On failure it returns the feasible current iterate and a best observed point if one has been observed, or none otherwise; it does not return a full-horizon average. If all calls succeed, the weighted average is defined and feasible, a best observed iterate exists, and the status is budget-exhausted after exactly $N$ updates.

**Given:** A nonempty closed convex feasible set, a finite budget, positive stepsizes, and the oracle/failure rules of [[alg-projected-subgradient-method]].

[F1] Every point has a unique nearest-point projection onto a nonempty closed convex set ([[thm-nearest-point-in-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]]).

[F2] A convex combination of feasible points remains feasible ([[thm-finite-jensen-inequality-in-euclidean-space]]).

[F3] A nonempty finite list of real values has a minimum attained at one of its members ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]); scanning the list in increasing index order and replacing the record only on a strict decrease yields the least-index minimizer, by induction on the finite list length.

[F4] A finite sum of nonnegative terms is nonnegative, and a zero sum forces every term to be zero; therefore a nonempty finite sum of strictly positive terms is strictly positive ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

## Proof

1.1 Initially $x_0\in C$. At each successful oracle call, if $x_k\in C$, [F1] gives a unique projected point $x_{k+1}\in C$. Induction over the successful calls proves feasibility and unique definition of each iterate through at most $N$ calls. [given, F1, induction]

2.1 A failed call returns immediately; if no earlier value was observed, the optional best field is none, and otherwise [F3] supplies a least-index best among the finite observed list. If all calls succeed, $N\ge1$ and every $\alpha_k>0$, so $A_N=\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k>0$ by [F4]. The weights $\alpha_k/A_N$ are positive and sum to one by the scaling law for finite sums; [F2] makes the weighted average feasible, and [F3] gives a least-index best observed point. The finite loop completes exactly $N$ updates and returns budget-exhausted. [given, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex; let $t>0$, $v\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $m_i(y)=b_i+\langle a_i,y\rangle$ be a nonempty finite list of affine functions. Then
$$\Phi(y)=\max_i m_i(y)+\frac{\|y-v\|_2^2}{2t},\qquad y\in C,$$
has a unique global minimizer on $C$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Closed convex feasibility ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]], [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]), the Euclidean norm and Cauchy–Schwarz ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]), closed bounded compactness ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]), and attainment on compact sets ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

[F1] A finite maximum of affine maps obeys $|\max_i m_i(y)-\max_i m_i(z)|\le\max_i|m_i(y)-m_i(z)|$; each difference is $|\langle a_i,y-z\rangle|\le\|a_i\|_2\|y-z\|_2$ by Cauchy–Schwarz ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]).

[F2] The quadratic difference obeys $|\|y-v\|_2^2-\|z-v\|_2^2|\le(\|y-v\|_2+\|z-v\|_2)\|y-z\|_2$, by expansion and Cauchy–Schwarz ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]).

[F3] Continuity in a metric space is the epsilon-delta property at every point ([[def-metric-continuity]]).

[F4] $\mathbb R^0$ consists of one vector, its zero vector ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

## Proof

1.1 If $n=0$, [F4] says $\mathbb R^0$ is a singleton, so the nonempty feasible set $C$ is that singleton. The finite maximum and quadratic objective have one feasible value, and its sole feasible point is the unique global minimizer. For the remainder assume $n\ge1$. [F4, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F1] and [F2], $\Phi$ has a finite local Lipschitz bound on $C$ around each point: the finitely many $\|a_i\|_2$ are bounded, and the quadratic difference in [F2] has a bounded factor on a sufficiently small ball. Hence $\Phi$ is continuous on $C$ by [F3]. Choose $y_0\in C$ and let $c=\Phi(y_0)$. The sublevel set $S=\{y\in C:\Phi(y)\le c\}$ is nonempty. If $y\in C\setminus S$, continuity supplies an ambient ball around $y$ whose intersection with $C$ lies in $C\setminus S$; if $y\notin C$, closedness of $C$ supplies a ball disjoint from $C$. Thus every point outside $S$ has a ball disjoint from $S$, so $S$ is closed in $\mathbb R^n$. [F1, F2, F3, given, choose]

3.1 The first affine cut gives $\Phi(y)\ge b_1+\langle a_1,y\rangle+\|y-v\|_2^2/(2t)=\beta+\|y-(v-ta_1)\|_2^2/(2t)$, where $\beta=b_1+\langle a_1,v\rangle-t\|a_1\|_2^2/2$. Since $c=\Phi(y_0)\ge\beta$, every $y\in S$ satisfies $\|y-(v-ta_1)\|_2^2\le2t(c-\beta)$ and thus lies in the open ball of radius $1+\sqrt{2t(c-\beta)}$ about $v-ta_1$. So $S$ is bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) and compact by Heine–Borel. The continuous real-valued restriction $\Phi|_S$ attains its minimum by the extreme-value theorem; points outside $S$ have value greater than $c$, while the minimum on $S$ is at most $c$, so this is a global minimizer. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For every index $i$, affinity gives $m_i((p+q)/2)=(m_i(p)+m_i(q))/2\le(\max_jm_j(p)+\max_jm_j(q))/2$; taking the finite maximum over $i$ proves the model midpoint value is at most the average endpoint values. For distinct $p,q\in C$, the quadratic term satisfies $\|(p+q)/2-v\|_2^2=(\|p-v\|_2^2+\|q-v\|_2^2)/2-\|p-q\|_2^2/4$. After multiplication by $1/(2t)$ the quadratic term is strictly below the endpoint average. If both $p,q$ minimized $\Phi$, their midpoint would therefore have smaller value, a contradiction. The minimizer is unique. [given, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

For a finite integer budget $N\ge1$, every invocation of [[alg-proximal-bundle-serious-null-method]] returns one of its specified statuses after at most $N$ trials. ## Statement

Consider an infinite continuation of the polling and mesh-update rules of [[alg-deterministic-direct-search]], using its admissible inputs and exact branch rules but with no finite poll-budget cap. Write its fixed finite positive-spanning poll list as $D$ and its forcing function as $\rho$. Suppose a subsequence of unsuccessful polls indexed by $k_j$ has $\Delta_{k_j}\to0$ and centers $x_{k_j}$ in a compact set $K\subseteq V$, where $V\subseteq U$ is open. Assume $f:U\to\mathbb R$ is totally differentiable at every point of $V$ and $\nabla f$ is $L$-Lipschitz there. Here an accumulation point means a limit of a subsequence in the Euclidean metric. Then every such point is stationary, meaning $\nabla f(\bar x)=0$. Compactness ensures at least one such accumulation point. This asymptotic claim concerns the untruncated continuation; a finite-budget return is not a stationarity certificate.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The poll and forcing rules [[alg-deterministic-direct-search]], positive angle [[lem-positive-spanning-poll-set-has-uniform-angle]], uniform neighborhood radius [[lem-compact-set-in-open-neighborhood-has-uniform-radius]], local descent [[lem-direct-search-local-descent-inequality]], and compact metric sequential compactness [[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]].

[F1] There is $\kappa_D>0$ with $\max_i(-\langle u,d_i\rangle)\ge\kappa_D$ for every unit vector $u$ ([[lem-positive-spanning-poll-set-has-uniform-angle]]).

[F2] For sufficiently short displacements from any center in compact $K$, the segment remains in $V$ ([[lem-compact-set-in-open-neighborhood-has-uniform-radius]]).

[F3] If the segment $[x,x+h]$ lies in $V$, then $f(x+h)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),h\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\|h\|_2^2$ ([[lem-direct-search-local-descent-inequality]]).

[F4] A sequence is a function on the naturals, convergence is the metric limit, and every sequence in compact metric $K$ has a subsequence converging in $K$ ([[def-sequence]], [[def-metric-convergence]], [[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]], [[def-metric-compactness]]).

[F5] On $\mathbb R^n$ with $n\ge1$, the Euclidean metric is $d_2(x,y)=\|x-y\|_2$; thus the $L$-Lipschitz hypothesis gives $\|\nabla f(u)-\nabla f(v)\|_2\le L\|u-v\|_2$ ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

[F6] The finite poll list has a largest norm $D_{\max}=\max_i\|d_i\|_2$ ([[def-positive-spanning-poll-set-and-angle]]).

## Proof

1.1 Use the defined finite maximum $D_{\max}$ from [F6], and choose the uniform radius $\delta>0$ from [F2]. For all sufficiently large $j$, $\Delta_{k_j}D_{\max}<\delta$, so every segment from $x_{k_j}$ to $x_{k_j}+\Delta_{k_j}d_i$ remains in $V. [F2, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 If $\nabla f(x_{k_j})\ne0$, [F1] supplies a poll direction $d_i$ with $\langle\nabla f(x_{k_j}),d_i\rangle\le-\kappa_D\|\nabla f(x_{k_j})\|_2$. The poll is unsuccessful, so its in-domain trial value is at least $f(x_{k_j})-\rho(\Delta_{k_j})$. Apply [F3] to this direction and combine the two bounds to obtain $\kappa_D\|\nabla f(x_{k_j})\|_2\le\rho(\Delta_{k_j})/\Delta_{k_j}+(L\Delta_{k_j}/2)D_{\max}^2$. If the gradient is zero, the same inequality holds. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The right side tends to zero by the forcing condition and $\Delta_{k_j}\to0$, while $\kappa_D>0$; hence $\|\nabla f(x_{k_j})\|_2\to0$. For any accumulation subsequence converging to $\bar x\in K$, [F5] gives $\|\nabla f(x_{k_j})-\nabla f(\bar x)\|_2\le L\|x_{k_j}-\bar x\|_2\to0$, so $\nabla f(\bar x)=0$. By [F4] at least one accumulation subsequence exists. [given, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex, and run [[alg-projected-subgradient-method]] for $N\ge1$ steps with positive $\alpha_k$. Assume all $N$ oracle calls return valid pairs. Suppose a global minimizer $x^*\in C$ exists and the oracle vectors obey $\|g_k\|_2\le G$; let $R\ge\|x_0-x^*\|_2$. Set $A_N=\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k>0$ and $\bar x_N=A_N^{-1}\sum_{k<N}\alpha_kx_k$. Then
$$\min_{0\le k<N}\bigl(f(x_k)-f(x^*)\bigr)\le f(\bar x_N)-f(x^*)\le\frac{R^2+G^2\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k^2}{2A_N}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite algorithm [[alg-projected-subgradient-method]], its one-step estimate [[lem-projected-subgradient-one-step-estimate]], convexity [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]], and finite Jensen [[thm-finite-jensen-inequality-in-euclidean-space]].

[F1] For each $k$, $\|x_{k+1}-x^*\|_2^2\le\|x_k-x^*\|_2^2-2\alpha_k(f(x_k)-f(x^*))+\alpha_k^2\|g_k\|_2^2$ ([[lem-projected-subgradient-one-step-estimate]]).

[F2] For a convex function and nonnegative weights summing to one, its value at the weighted average is at most the weighted average of its values ([[thm-finite-jensen-inequality-in-euclidean-space]]).

[F3] Starting from $x_0\in C$, each successful update is the unique projection onto $C$ and remains feasible; the finite-budget result also establishes that the returned average is defined and feasible ([[alg-projected-subgradient-method]], [[thm-nearest-point-in-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]], [[lem-projected-subgradient-finite-budget-returns-status]]).

[F4] Since the stepsizes are positive, $A_N=\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k>0$, and the weights $\alpha_k/A_N$ are positive and sum to one by the scaling law for finite sums ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

[F5] The nonempty finite list of objective gaps has a minimum attained by one of its indices ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

## Proof

1.1 Rearrange [F1] and sum over $k=0,\ldots,N-1$. The squared-distance terms telescope, giving $2\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k(f(x_k)-f(x^*))\le\|x_0-x^*\|_2^2-\|x_N-x^*\|_2^2+\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k^2\|g_k\|_2^2\le R^2+G^2\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k^2$, since the last squared distance is nonnegative. Divide by $2A_N>0$ using [F4] to bound the weighted average of the objective gaps. [F1, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F3] the iterates lie in $C$, and by [F4] the normalized positive weights sum to one. Apply [F2] to get $f(\bar x_N)-f(x^*)\le A_N^{-1}\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k(f(x_k)-f(x^*))$. By [F5], the minimum gap is attained; since a positive weighted average with weights summing to one is at least the minimum term, combining with step 1.1 proves both inequalities. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

$$\min_{k<N}(f(x_k)-f(x^*))\le f(\bar x_N)-f(x^*)\le\frac{RG}{\sqrt N}.$$

**Given:** The best-iterate and weighted-average bound [[thm-projected-subgradient-best-and-average-bound]].

[F1] The bound is $[R^2+G^2\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k^2]/(2\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k)$ ([[thm-projected-subgradient-best-and-average-bound]]).

[F2] The Euclidean norm is definite, so $\|v\|_2=0$ implies $v=0$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]).

## Statement

Let $F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed, and convex, with nonempty closed convex domain $C=\operatorname{dom}F$. Fix $t>0$, a center $x\in C$, and a finite affine model $M\le F$ on $C$. Let $z$ minimize $M(y)+\|y-x\|_2^2/(2t)$ over $C$, set $e=F(z)-M(z)\ge0$, and let $p=\operatorname{prox}_{tF}(x)$. Then
$$\|z-p\|_2^2\le4te.$$
In particular, a sequence of such model errors $e_k\to0$ forces the model candidates to approach their exact proximal points in norm.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Bundle subproblem existence [[lem-proximal-bundle-subproblem-has-unique-minimizer]], proximal mapping [[def-proximal-mapping]], resolvent/existence [[thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive]], and quadratic growth [[lem-proximal-objective-has-quadratic-growth-from-minimizer]].

[F2] The convex function $Q_F$ obeys $Q_F(z)\ge Q_F(p)+\|z-p\|_2^2/(4t)$ ([[lem-proximal-objective-has-quadratic-growth-from-minimizer]]).

## Proof

2.1 Apply [F2] to $z$ and combine with step 1.1: $Q_F(p)+\|z-p\|_2^2/(4t)\le Q_F(z)\le Q_F(p)+e$. Subtracting the common finite value and multiplying by $4t>0$ proves the inequality. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Consider an infinite full-memory continuation of [[alg-proximal-bundle-serious-null-method]] with fixed $t>0$ and $m_s\in(0,1)$, centers $x_k\in C$, finite affine models $M_k\le F$ on $C$ touching their centers ($M_k(x_k)=F(x_k)$), and exact candidates
$$z_k=\arg\min_{y\in C}\left(M_k(y)+\frac{\|y-x_k\|_2^2}{2t}\right).$$
Assume every predicted decrease $P_k=F(x_k)-M_k(z_k)$ is positive, each trial uses the stated serious/null acceptance test, the initial sublevel set $K=\{x\in C:F(x)\le F(x_0)\}$ is compact, and the aggregate-model errors $e_k=F(z_k)-M_k(z_k)$ satisfy $e_k\to0$. Then every accumulation point, meaning a limit of a subsequence in the Euclidean metric, is a global minimizer of $F$. At least one accumulation point exists. ## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The serious/null algorithm [[alg-proximal-bundle-serious-null-method]], model-subproblem existence [[lem-proximal-bundle-subproblem-has-unique-minimizer]], the aggregate-error estimate [[lem-aggregate-model-error-controls-proximal-candidate]], proximal resolvent [[thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive]], extended-real subgradient definition [[def-extended-real-epsilon-subdifferential]], compact sequential compactness [[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]], and attainment on compact metric spaces [[thm-extreme-value-metric]].

[F1] Each candidate is unique, and the exact proximal point $p_k=\operatorname{prox}_{tF}(x_k)$ exists, is unique, and the proximal map is nonexpansive ([[lem-proximal-bundle-subproblem-has-unique-minimizer]], [[def-proximal-mapping]], [[thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive]]).

[F2] The model error is nonnegative and $\|z_k-p_k\|_2^2\le4te_k$ ([[lem-aggregate-model-error-controls-proximal-candidate]]).

[F3] If $0\in\partial F(x)$, then $F(y)\ge F(x)$ for every $y$ by the extended-real subgradient definition ([[def-extended-real-epsilon-subdifferential]]).

[F4] A sequence is a function on the naturals, convergence is the metric limit, and every sequence in compact $K$ has a subsequence converging in $K$ ([[def-sequence]], [[def-metric-convergence]], [[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]], [[def-metric-compactness]]).
